bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material price volatility — Heat exchangers are manufactured using copper, stainless steel and aluminium, whose prices remain highly volatile on global commodity cycles, nickel price movements and energy costs; copper prices in particular rose sharply during FY 2025-26. Copper, aluminium and steel together constitute a substantial majority of the bill of materials, so margins are directly exposed to commodity cycles. Mitigated by supplier diversification, strategic inventory buffers of approximately 2.5 months, evaluation of forward contracts and alternate sourcing, and quarterly settlement and pass-through of metal pricing to customers.
- Capacity utilisation and project execution risk at the new HVAC Products facility — A meaningful part of the growth outlook is linked to progressive utilisation of newly commissioned capacity at the HVAC Products facility, which remains in the early stages of ramp-up; slower-than-anticipated customer qualification, order conversion or execution could affect the pace of revenue growth. Mitigated by a structured, phased utilisation roadmap, active customer qualification, a quality management system and continued new-customer additions across domestic and export markets.
- Customer concentration risk — A degree of dependence on a limited number of large OEM customers poses a risk of revenue fluctuation from order cancellations, delays or contract non-renewal. Mitigated by diversifying the customer base across domestic and international markets and deepening long-term relationships through continuous improvement in product and service quality.
- Dependence on imported critical minerals — High-performance alloys used in heat exchangers depend on critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earth elements, whose global processing capacity is highly concentrated, with China accounting for over 90% of rare earth processing. Mitigated by close supply chain monitoring and evaluation of sourcing-market diversification to reduce dependence on any single geography.
- Foreign exchange risk — Import of raw materials and export revenue expose the Company to currency fluctuations affecting costs and profitability, particularly amid elevated global volatility linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict. Mitigated through hedging strategies such as forward exchange contracts and periodic review of procurement and pricing strategies.
- Geopolitical and supply chain risk — The ongoing Middle East conflict continues to disrupt global shipping routes, elevate freight and insurance costs, and create broader input cost volatility affecting the industry. Mitigated by close monitoring of global supply chain developments and maintaining flexibility in sourcing and logistics arrangements.
- Competitive intensity in the Indian HVAC&R market — Intense competitive pressures from established domestic and international players operating in the Indian HVAC&R market, listed by management as a threat in the SWOT analysis, constrain pricing power in a business already exposed to commodity-driven cost pass-through.
- Regulatory compliance and technology obsolescence risk — The Board's Report identifies regulations, competition, business risk, technology obsolescence, investments, retention of talent and expansion of facilities as the common risks to accomplishing growth plans, with business risk including financial, political, fidelity and legal risk. The Company is exposed to market risk, credit risk, liquidity risk, regulatory risk, human resource risk and commodity price risk, overseen by a Risk Management Committee constituted during the year under Regulation 21 of the Listing Regulations.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was defined by a structural leap in manufacturing footprint. KRN's existing Plant I in the RIICO Industrial Area at Neemrana, Rajasthan covers 100,000 square feet and ran at high utilisation through the year — 84.00% for evaporator and condenser coils, 84.53% for copper headers and 85.77% for sheet metal components. To remove that constraint the Company inaugurated Plant II, a state-of-the-art HVAC products facility built under its wholly-owned subsidiary KRN HVAC Products Private Limited (KRNSPH), spanning roughly 700,000 square feet at Neemrana and commissioned in May 2025. Management describes it as a six-fold capacity expansion taking scaled total production capacity to approximately over 6 million units per annum, funded substantially out of IPO proceeds, with the plant still in the early stages of its utilisation ramp-up and a structured, phased utilisation roadmap in place. The Company now operates three manufacturing facilities on a single centralised campus at Neemrana — one dedicated to heating and refrigeration products and two to HVAC products — alongside a dedicated R&D centre, the Thermotech Research Laboratory, which carries 15+ advanced test systems and a psychrometric facility rated up to 55 TR. BRSR Section A reports 5 plants and 6 offices (6 service centres) nationally and none internationally. The second expansion axis was inorganic: through an asset-and-team acquisition in Q2 FY 2025-26 KRN absorbed the bus air-conditioning division of Sphere Refrigeration Systems, bringing technical know-how, intellectual property and an experienced operating team, and moving the Company from component supplier to fully integrated system assembler in the pan-India bus AC market. Funding for the next phase came from a ₹350 crore Qualified Institutional Placement closed in mid-2026, backed by institutional investors including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, intended to fund multi-fold capacity expansion and incremental working capital. Within the subsidiary structure, KRN converted a ₹100 crore unsecured inter-corporate loan to KRN HVAC Products into equity during the year, and after year-end subscribed in full to that subsidiary's rights issue, retaining 100% ownership. Forward-looking expansion themes management names are continued scaling of manufacturing capacity across HVAC, refrigeration, data centres, automotive, railways and industrial cooling, and diversification into new product lines including printed circuit heat exchangers, microchannel and hybrid heat exchangers, and modular thermal management systems.

- Indian HVAC market projected to expand from approximately USD 17.1 billion in FY 2025 to USD 32.6 billion by FY 2030, a CAGR of approximately 13.7%, driven by rising cooling demand and rising room air-conditioner penetration
- Global heat exchanger market projected to grow from approximately USD 21.4 billion in CY 2026E to USD 29.6 billion by CY 2030 at approximately 8.5% CAGR, with Asia-Pacific emerging as the leading region by CY 2030
- Data centre and semiconductor expansion: Indian data centres rose from 130 in CY 2021 to 271 in CY 2025 with cumulative investment of approximately USD 95 billion, and cooling infrastructure constitutes 15-25% of total data centre capital expenditure, particularly as the sector shifts toward liquid and hybrid cooling
- Infrastructure-led capital expenditure, with a record Union Budget 2026-27 capital outlay of approximately ₹12.2 lakh Crore plus NICDP, PM GatiShakti and the Integrated East Coast Industrial Corridor sustaining demand for thermal management equipment
- Transportation electrification, including the PM e-Bus Sewa Scheme's sanction of 10,000 air-conditioned electric buses across 116 cities, sustaining HVAC demand in the transport segment
- India's heat exchange equipment trade shifting from net importer to net exporter, plus improving cost competitiveness and FTAs including the India-EU FTA and India-Oman CEPA, supporting export growth
- Cold chain and warehousing headroom, with warehousing stock at approximately 610.0 million sq ft in CY 2025 projected to reach 850 million sq ft by CY 2030 and cold storage capacity constrained relative to demand
- Renewable energy integration, with India's installed renewable capacity rising from 95.8 GW in FY 2021 to approximately 275.4 GW as of February 2026, creating heat-exchanger demand in concentrated solar, hydrogen and battery storage cooling
- Pharmaceutical sector growth, with India's pharma turnover projected to reach ₹8 lakh Crore by FY 2030 driving demand for precision HVAC and cleanroom thermal control
- Margin lever: revenue growth continued to significantly outpace the global heat exchanger market CAGR of approximately 8.0% and the Indian market CAGR of approximately 10.4%, reflecting market share gains and improving operating leverage
- Margin headwind: copper prices in particular rose sharply during FY 2025-26 alongside stainless steel and aluminium, mitigated by an inventory buffer of approximately 2.5 months and quarterly settlement and pass-through to customers for metal pricing

- Government policy support through PLI schemes, the National Capital Goods Policy and Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Capital Goods Sector (Phase-II), the Boilers Act 2025, and the ECBC and Standards & Labelling programmes
- Geopolitical headwind: the Israel/United States-Iran conflict from February 2026 has disrupted Strait of Hormuz flows, elevated freight and insurance costs and extended Asia-Europe lead times by 10-14 days
- Commercial integration roadmap for the bus AC segment: 10 to 15 new bus AC customers added, commercial supply commenced to a first major OEM, and a non-disclosure agreement signed with a primary anchor customer in FY 2026-27
- Management states the new capacity gives KRN the backbone to undertake large, multi-year contracts and fulfil large-scale global supply contracts, without disclosing an order-book value

currentContext.expansion: FY 2025-26 was defined by a structural leap in manufacturing footprint. KRN's existing Plant I in the RIICO Industrial Area at Neemrana, Rajasthan covers 100,000 square feet and ran at high utilisation through the year — 84.00% for evaporator and condenser coils, 84.53% for copper headers and 85.77% for sheet metal components. To remove that constraint the Company inaugurated Plant II, a state-of-the-art HVAC products facility built under its wholly-owned subsidiary KRN HVAC Products Private Limited (KRNSPH), spanning roughly 700,000 square feet at Neemrana and commissioned in May 2025. Management describes it as a six-fold capacity expansion taking scaled total production capacity to approximately over 6 million units per annum, funded substantially out of IPO proceeds, with the plant still in the early stages of its utilisation ramp-up and a structured, phased utilisation roadmap in place. The Company now operates three manufacturing facilities on a single centralised campus at Neemrana — one dedicated to heating and refrigeration products and two to HVAC products — alongside a dedicated R&D centre, the Thermotech Research Laboratory, which carries 15+ advanced test systems and a psychrometric facility rated up to 55 TR. BRSR Section A reports 5 plants and 6 offices (6 service centres) nationally and none internationally. The second expansion axis was inorganic: through an asset-and-team acquisition in Q2 FY 2025-26 KRN absorbed the bus air-conditioning division of Sphere Refrigeration Systems, bringing technical know-how, intellectual property and an experienced operating team, and moving the Company from component supplier to fully integrated system assembler in the pan-India bus AC market. Funding for the next phase came from a ₹350 crore Qualified Institutional Placement closed in mid-2026, backed by institutional investors including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, intended to fund multi-fold capacity expansion and incremental working capital. Within the subsidiary structure, KRN converted a ₹100 crore unsecured inter-corporate loan to KRN HVAC Products into equity during the year, and after year-end subscribed in full to that subsidiary's rights issue, retaining 100% ownership. Forward-looking expansion themes management names are continued scaling of manufacturing capacity across HVAC, refrigeration, data centres, automotive, railways and industrial cooling, and diversification into new product lines including printed circuit heat exchangers, microchannel and hybrid heat exchangers, and modular thermal management systems.

risks.note: Heat exchangers are manufactured using copper, stainless steel and aluminium, whose prices remain highly volatile on global commodity cycles, nickel price movements and energy costs; copper prices in particular rose sharply during FY 2025-26. Copper, aluminium and steel together constitute a substantial majority of the bill of materials, so margins are directly exposed to commodity cycles. Mitigated by supplier diversification, strategic inventory buffers of approximately 2.5 months, evaluation of forward contracts and alternate sourcing, and quarterly settlement and pass-through of metal pricing to customers.

risks.risk: Capacity utilisation and project execution risk at the new HVAC Products facility
risks.note: A meaningful part of the growth outlook is linked to progressive utilisation of newly commissioned capacity at the HVAC Products facility, which remains in the early stages of ramp-up; slower-than-anticipated customer qualification, order conversion or execution could affect the pace of revenue growth. Mitigated by a structured, phased utilisation roadmap, active customer qualification, a quality management system and continued new-customer additions across domestic and export markets.

A degree of dependence on a limited number of large OEM customers poses a risk of revenue fluctuation from order cancellations, delays or contract non-renewal. Mitigated by diversifying the customer base across domestic and international markets and deepening long-term relationships through continuous improvement in product and service quality.

High-performance alloys used in heat exchangers depend on critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earth elements, whose global processing capacity is highly concentrated, with China accounting for over 90% of rare earth processing. Mitigated by close supply chain monitoring and evaluation of sourcing-market diversification to reduce dependence on any single geography.

Import of raw materials and export revenue expose the Company to currency fluctuations affecting costs and profitability, particularly amid elevated global volatility linked to the ongoing Middle East conflict. Mitigated through hedging strategies such as forward exchange contracts and periodic review of procurement and pricing strategies.

The ongoing Middle East conflict continues to disrupt global shipping routes, elevate freight and insurance costs, and create broader input cost volatility affecting the industry. Mitigated by close monitoring of global supply chain developments and maintaining flexibility in sourcing and logistics arrangements.

- Transportation electrification, including the PM e-Bus Sewa Scheme's sanction of 10,000 air-conditioned electric buses across 116 cities, sustaining HVAC demand in the transport segment
- India's heat exchange equipment trade shifting from net importer to net exporter, plus improving cost competitiveness and FTAs including the India-EU FTA and India-Oman CEPA, supporting export growth
- Cold chain and warehousing headroom, with warehousing stock at approximately 610.0 million sq ft in CY 2025 projected to reach 850 million sq ft by CY 2030 and cold storage capacity constrained relative to demand
- Renewable energy integration, with India's installed renewable capacity rising from 95.8 GW in FY 2021 to approximately 275.4 GW as of February 2026, creating heat-exchanger demand in concentrated solar, hydrogen and battery storage cooling
- Pharmaceutical sector growth, with India's pharma turnover projected to reach ₹8 lakh Crore by FY 2030 driving demand for precision HVAC and cleanroom thermal control
- Margin lever: revenue growth continued to significantly outpace the global heat exchanger market CAGR of approximately 8.0% and the Indian market CAGR of approximately 10.4%, reflecting market share gains and improving operating leverage
- Margin headwind: copper prices in particular rose sharply during FY 2025-26 alongside stainless steel and aluminium, mitigated by an inventory buffer of approximately 2.5 months and quarterly settlement and pass-through to customers for metal pricing
- Near-term growth is contingent on the progressive utilisation of newly commissioned capacity at the HVAC Products facility, which remains in the early stages of its utilisation ramp-up
- Government policy support through PLI schemes, the National Capital Goods Policy and Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Capital Goods Sector (Phase-II), the Boilers Act 2025, and the ECBC and Standards & Labelling programmes
- Geopolitical headwind: the Israel/United States-Iran conflict from February 2026 has disrupted Strait of Hormuz flows, elevated freight and insurance costs and extended Asia-Europe lead times by 10-14 days
- Commercial integration roadmap for the bus AC segment: 10 to 15 new bus AC customers added, commercial supply commenced to a first major OEM, and a non-disclosure agreement signed with a primary anchor customer in FY 2026-27
- Management states the new capacity gives KRN the backbone to undertake large, multi-year contracts and fulfil large-scale global supply contracts, without disclosing an order-book value

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY 2025-26 was defined by a structural leap in manufacturing footprint. KRN's existing Plant I in the RIICO Industrial Area at Neemrana, Rajasthan covers 100,000 square feet and ran at high utilisation through the year — 84.00% for evaporator and condenser coils, 84.53% for copper headers and 85.77% for sheet metal components. To remove that constraint the Company inaugurated Plant II, a state-of-the-art HVAC products facility built under its wholly-owned subsidiary KRN HVAC Products Private Limited (KRNSPH), spanning roughly 700,000 square feet at Neemrana and commissioned in May 2025. Management describes it as a six-fold capacity expansion taking scaled total production capacity to approximately over 6 million units per annum, funded substantially out of IPO proceeds, with the plant still in the early stages of its utilisation ramp-up and a structured, phased utilisation roadmap in place. The Company now operates three manufacturing facilities on a single centralised campus at Neemrana — one dedicated to heating and refrigeration products and two to HVAC products — alongside a dedicated R&D centre, the Thermotech Research Laboratory, which carries 15+ advanced test systems and a psychrometric facility rated up to 55 TR. BRSR Section A reports 5 plants and 6 offices (6 service centres) nationally and none internationally. The second expansion axis was inorganic: through an asset-and-team acquisition in Q2 FY 2025-26 KRN absorbed the bus air-conditioning division of Sphere Refrigeration Systems, bringing technical know-how, intellectual property and an experienced operating team, and moving the Company from component supplier to fully integrated system assembler in the pan-India bus AC market. Funding for the next phase came from a ₹350 crore Qualified Institutional Placement closed in mid-2026, backed by institutional investors including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, intended to fund multi-fold capacity expansion and incremental working capital. Within the subsidiary structure, KRN converted a ₹100 crore unsecured inter-corporate loan to KRN HVAC Products into equity during the year, and after year-end subscribed in full to that subsidiary's rights issue, retaining 100% ownership. Forward-looking expansion themes management names are continued scaling of manufacturing capacity across HVAC, refrigeration, data centres, automotive, railways and industrial cooling, and diversification into new product lines including printed circuit heat exchangers, microchannel and hybrid heat exchangers, and modular thermal management systems.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Highly confident on long-term structural growth (Data Center, Bus AC); transparent about short-term working capital inefficiencies; aggressive on market share capture (15% in Bus AC); cautious on precise near-term numbers due to ramp-up variables.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Integrated thermal and HVAC&R platform with a broad-based portfolio across 9 product categories serving 19 end-use application categories, spanning HVAC, refrigeration, data centres, automotive, railways, industrial cooling and process applications
- Diversified, marquee customer base of over 200 customers globally, including Daikin, Schneider Electric, Carrier, Voltas, Blue Star, Knorr-Bremse and Trosten, reducing dependence on any single customer relationship
- Scaled and expanding manufacturing footprint, with three facilities at Neemrana, Rajasthan supported by integrated production, testing and quality-control infrastructure
- Established export franchise across 19 countries, including North America, Europe and UAE, with exports contributing an increasing share of consolidated revenue
- Quality and certification moat, with 10 or more certifications and product approvals, supported by stringent in-house testing capability including 100% automated helium leak and pressure-burst testing
- Dedicated technology and R&D capability through the Thermotech Research Laboratory, with 15+ advanced test systems and a psychrometric facility of up to 55 TR capacity, supporting proprietary product engineering and customised solutions
- Vertical integration across raw materials, critical components and full-system manufacturing, together with advanced nano and powder coatings for corrosion resistance
- Quarterly settlement and pass-through arrangements with customers for metal pricing, cushioning commodity volatility

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Working Capital Strain: Inventory days elevated to ~2.5 months due to logistics delays and new product stocking. Regulatory: BIS certification delays for inner groove tubes impacting imports. Geopolitical: Freight cost volatility and dispatch delays to UAE. Execution: Ramp-up speed of 8 new product lines.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: The inventory buildup is largely strategic (BIS hedging) and logistical (UAE dispatch delay) rather than demand weakness; Rs.8cr of March exports are already shipped but unbilled, artificially inflating inventory and depressing Q4 revenue recognition. The company is effectively a 'hidden' liquid cooling play via its development of plate heat exchangers for CDUs.

themes.need: AI/data-center capex pulls transformers, switchgear, gensets, HVAC/cooling, optical and cabling AND a new high-margin cooling supply chain.
